articles.content:
Penélope Cruz, who is emerging as a major contender in this year’s Oscar race with a trio of films, is set to star and produce “Patricia,” a Netflix drama written and directed by Juan Diego Botto.

Set to start filming soon, "Patricia" marks the first narrative feature produced by Moonlyon, the production company Cruz launched in partnership with Imagina.

The film reteams Cruz with Botto following his feature debut “On the Fringes,” a socially minded drama. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Jimmy Kimmel Calls for Donald Trump to Resign Amid Republicans’ Midterm Elections Losses: ‘Quit Already … Nobody Wants You’ Trump Rages That ‘60 Minutes’ Current Leadership Is 'Even Worse Than Their Predecessors,' Claims Newsmagazine's Iran Whistleblower Report Lacked Context

Cruz stars as Patricia, a woman who escapes a 12-year abusive relationship only to find herself facing another ordeal in the courts, where she fears for the well-being of her children.

The cast also includes Goya Toledo (“Amores Perros,” “Marsella”), Ramón Barea (“Lullaby,” “Everybody Knows”) and Dylan Radley.

“After two years of writing and a long research process, which included hours of interviews with women who trusted us with their stories, it is a privilege for me to tell this story with this cast and this creative team,” Botto said.

Cruz said she had also been involved in developing “Patricia” alongside Botto for over two years.

”I feel enormous excitement,” Cruz said. “It has been a beautiful and intense journey alongside my dear Juan Diego Botto. Juan has written a wonderful script, and it is an honor to tell this story with him.”

“It is a very necessary story, and an immense privilege to play this character. Patricia represents so many other women who, like her, suffer this kind of violence every day,” she continued. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The actor also praised Netflix’s Spanish team. “This is my first film with them, and we couldn’t be happier with the care and attention they have shown us,” she said.

Diego Ávalos, Netflix’s VP of content for Spain, Portugal, Turkey and the Middle East, highlighted the film's international resonance.

“Some stories matter to us for what they tell and how they are told, and Patricia is one of those rare and unforgettable stories: brave and courageous, brought to life by an extraordinary team,” Ávalos said. “I’m truly honored to join Juan Diego Botto and Penélope Cruz in their first film for Netflix in Spain, and for a story born at home to move audiences here and around the world.”

articles.title: 4 MCU Deaths That Could Happen in Avengers: Doomsday, And 1 Would Change the Entire Franchise
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel As Avengers: Doomsday draws closer and closer, fans are preparing themselves for a potential mourning. Some deaths were for good, with Natasha Romanov and Tony Stark in Avengers: Endgame, while other characters were […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google As Avengers: Doomsday draws closer and closer, fans are preparing themselves for a potential mourning. Past Avengers films haven’t shied away from killing off team members, no matter how much of a fan favorite they may be. Some deaths were for good, with Natasha Romanov and Tony Stark in Avengers: Endgame, while other characters were able to come back, with The Vision in Avengers: Infinity War and Wanda Maximoff in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

Some characters are safe — Peter Parker isn’t slated to return to the MCU until Avengers: Secret Wars, while Black Panther III has already confirmed the return of Shuri and M’Baku. It also seems unlikely for the Marvel Cinematic Universe to kill off Florence Pugh’s Yelena Belova, especially with the star power she’s lent to Black Widow, Hawkeye, Thunderbolts, and one of the most successful films of the year, Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

Still, given the inherent danger of the incursions and Doctor Doom’s plan to set the universe right, there’s no way everybody is getting out of Doomsday alive. Doomsday is the confirmed last appearance for Patrick Stewart as Charles Xavier, and it’d make sense if his fellow X-Men also aren’t returning for future movies. Loki, despite his star status, also feels like he can only cheat death so many more times.

I’d be surprised if Scott Lang makes it out of Avengers: Doomsday alive. His last film, Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, was a flop and can be easily discarded given the pivot away from Kang. There’s also the matter of the discourse around his flub about Captain America. The MCU spent so much time trying to build up Sam Wilson as Captain America through both The Falcon and the Winter Soldier and Captain America: Brave New World , yet it can’t resist a gag where Scott Lang doesn’t know what to call Steve Rogers.

Killing off Scott Lang also enables his daughter, Cassie Lang, to step into a larger role in the MCU. Aside from showing off the large cast, the Doomsday teases have focused on the motif of parenthood — Steve with his kid, Thor with his daughter — and with that, there’s been a frequently played scene with Scott and Cassie. Scott’s bond with Cassie was a main focus of the Ant-Man franchise, and it’d be shocking if they’d killed her off and left Scott alive. Killing him off gives Cassie Lang extra motivation — his memory can inspire her to lead the next generation of heroes as part of the Young Avengers.

There would certainly be jokes to be made if Doomsday killed off both of their Scotts; that’s for sure. Aside from that, another Scott death wouldn’t be too shocking. While I’d assume he’d last longer than he did in X3: The Last Stand — where filming conflicts forced the writers’ hand to kill Summers off early — Scott Summers meeting his end could make sense. In terms of “stolen lives” and timeline confusion, what better example of that is there than the X-Men franchise? It often even confuses its own fans. Despite the initial X-films arguing for Scott Summers as one of Xavier’s first students along with Jean and Storm, the 2010s films instead position his younger brother Alex as a first student of Xavier’s, with Scott not entering the picture until X-Men: Apocalypse.

It’s unclear just how much of the X-Men timeline and lore Avengers: Doomsday will touch. It’s only a partial cast from the first three movies that are returning — plus Deadpool and Wolverine’s Gambit, played by Channing Tatum — with uncertainty regarding Famke Janssen’s Jean Grey . Still, Marsden appears to be leading his team of X-Men, and there’s nothing more Scott Summers than going down fighting, even if it means it’s to the death.

Would there be fan outrage? Yes. Do I think the MCU would kill off this character anyway? Yes. If this movie is to have real stakes, as fans are expected to believe, it can’t just be the expected characters dying. Given a new slate of actors for the X-Men, audiences know the original cast is hardly making it out of this movie, or if they do, they’ll be rebooted out of existence by Secret Wars. Loki, however, would make things real. 

It would hardly be the first time Loki’s died — so, it would likely get a level of disbelief from fans. Especially in the aftermath of Scarlet Witch’s retconned survival, fans might not believe that Loki really died. Thor: Ragnarok saw Thor reckoning with his brother’s faked death, and Avengers: Infinity War saw him get his neck crushed by Thanos, leading the main Loki in MCU continuity to be a variant, not the original. Loki’s a popular character, with the ratings to back it up, but Doctor Doom managing to kill a God would surely prove that he’s more dangerous than Thanos.

In terms of current anchor characters for the MCU, one of the main ones is Sebastian Stan’s Bucky Barnes. The character has been popular since his introduction and has consistently pushed the narrative forward. His time as the Winter Soldier led to the death of Tony Stark’s parents, and his history with Steve Rogers gained him a loyalty so strong that the then Captain America was willing to go against everybody in order to protect him. Bucky Barnes then managed to go from public enemy no. 1 to receiving a pardon from the U.S. government and getting elected to office in the House of Representatives.

Killing off Bucky would undoubtedly set off ricochets throughout the rest of the MCU, but could be a glue to merge the Thunderbolts and Avengers together. Captain America: Brave New World saw Sam Wilson asked to reform the Avengers, while Thunderbolts saw a new crew of heroes take up the mantle of the New Avengers. Wilson was hardly a fan of the New Avengers despite his friendship with Barnes, and the teams will likely be on not-great terms when we catch up with them in Doomsday. They’re likely to reach a tentative peace, especially with the larger foe of Doom to deal with, but sometimes nothing makes people put differences aside more than honoring somebody’s memory.

The UK government minister responsible for film and TV has made a personal plea to YouTube to "set an example" and remove Russell Brand 's channel.

Earlier, and under pressure, the Google-owned behemoth said it was investigating the video in which Brand's wife Laura protested his innocence via a statement he sent her from prison.

The UK government has previously called this video "appalling" and YouTube said it was investigating at the same time as Murray was speaking at the British Screen Forum Conference in London. Murray said the Brand issue has "highlighted what we've known going all the way back to the proliferation of these cases."

"It's morally repugnant that we are still having these discussions today when we've been having them for 25 to 30 years," he added. "I plead with everyone to sort it out and make everyone safe."

Some are calling on the UK government to intervene with legislation but Murray stressed the problem goes beyond this and needs the industry as a whole to take action. His boss, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, convened a meeting of industry leaders earlier this week.

"It's gone on for too long," added Murray. "We are ruining people's lives. It shouldn't take brave women to come forward for something to be done about this."

UK consdiering implications of U.S. tax incentive

Elsewhere, the UK government is keeping a firm eye on the proposed U.S. federal tax incentive for film and TV, added Murray.

Ian Murray said "we take the implications incredibly seriously" of the proposed 20% credit, which Donald Trump just gave his full-throated backing. He stressed that the outcome "remain to be seen."

Murray didn't elaborate on his concerns but presumably fears the UK could lose production to America if the credit gets rubberstamped. Murray said: "This is a healthy sector but it's fragile, so we are working closely with industry supporting a stronger domestic sector while welcoming inwards investment and the benefit that brings."

In September, the first-of-its-kind tax credit was introduced by a bipartisan group of lawmakers to create a 20% federal film and TV incentive, which is designed to lure production back to the U.S.

Earlier this week, Trump lent his backing , saying meetings are being set up with leaders of both parties to “get this done!"

Government "fundamentally rejects prospect of smaller BBC"

Murray and his team are in the process of negotiating a new charter with the BBC and he said today the government's white paper in the area is coming soon.

He was vociferous in his backing for allowing the BBC to "survive and thrive," noting that the government "fundamentally rejects the prospect of a smaller BBC," while urging the industry to be more public in supporting the nation's 100-year-old broadcaster.

"We lose it at our peril," said Murray. "If we value it we must vocally say that we back it. That’s my plea to you this morning."

With a new version of BBC iPlayer currently being tested, Murray said it should be the "world's leading platform for video delivery" and should be "democratized." New DG Matt Brittin has previously spoken of a YouTube-style "public service algorithm" connected to iPlayer.

Murray was speaking at the British Screen Forum in London. Later will be keynotes from BBC deputy boss Rhodri Talfan Davies and Ken Loach's producing partner Rebecca O'Brien.

articles.title: YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content
articles.summary: YouTube has turned down a request from the British government to remove a video in which Russell Brand claims he is innocent after being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault, according to the BBC. Google, which owns YouTube, said the video did not violate its rules and […]
articles.content:
YouTube has turned down a request from the British government to remove a video in which Russell Brand claims he is innocent after being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault, according to the BBC .

Google, which owns YouTube, said the video did not violate its rules and revealed it was reviewing the content.

“We are aware of the new content and our teams are investigating,” Google told the BBC in a statement. “We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then,” the company added. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Bill Maher Fires Back at Trump by Comparing Him to Taylor Swift Judge Refuses to Dismiss Trump's $10 Billion Defamation Suit Against BBC

The controversy follows a YouTube video posted Sunday by Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, in which she addressed the comedian’s conviction before reading a message from him during their “Sunday Service with the Brands” series.

“As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening,” Brand said in the message.

Gallacher also told viewers that her husband was “okay” and “praying” in prison. The couple, who married in 2017, share three children.

The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that YouTube remove the video, arguing that it was offensive to Brand’s victims and had reached a substantial audience.

British prison authorities are also investigating whether Brand breached prison rules by issuing the statement. Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he expected action to be taken if Brand was found to have violated regulations.

articles.title: Senate And House Lawmakers Added As Cosponsors To New Federal Film & TV Incentive Legislation

articles.content:
More than 60 House members and four Senators have signed on to legislation to establish a 20% federal film incentive, amid an effort to see passage during the lame duck session of Congress .

The new cosponsors in the Senate include Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC), Sen. Katie Britt (R-AL) and Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL). On the House side, boosters pointed to a long list of new co-sponsors that include Democrats such as Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-WA) and Rep. Josh Gottheimer, and Republicans such as Rep. Ken Calvert (R-CA) and Rep. Vince Fong (R-CA).

The legislation, the Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act , was introduced in September by Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) and, in the House, by Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Rep. Linda Sánchez (D-CA), Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) and Laura Friedman (D-CA). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); } Related Stories News Elon Musk Feels "Pretty Foolish" For Donating Mega-Bucks To Losing MAGA In Midterms News Newsmax Files Antitrust Lawsuit Against Fox Corp. The prospects for passage during the lame duck appear to hinge on attaching the legislation to a year-end funding bill or tax legislation, rather than as a standalone measure. A challenge has been the set of priorities of Republicans in their waning weeks in the leadership, with the Senate devoting substantial floor time to getting through President Donald Trump 's nominees.

Trump announced last summer that he is backing the legislation, giving the long gestating proposal a boost. Following the Republicans' midterm drubbing, Trump has tried to give the bill's prospects a boost by urging lawmakers to "get this done" in a social media post.

The bill also has the recently announced support of groups including the AFL-CIO, American Hotel and Lodging Association, the American Entertainment Alliance, The Internet and Television Association, and the Laborers’ International Union of North America.

Britt said in a statement that "for too long, countries have used aggressive incentives to lure American production companies, and the jobs that come with them, overseas. This bipartisan legislation would level the playing field and reward companies for bringing production back home. I’m proud to join my colleagues in this effort." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Durbin said, "We should be doing everything we can to ensure that these productions stay in the United States rather than move overseas to take advantage of more competitive incentives."

If the bill doesn't pass during the lame duck, it will have to be reintroduced in the next Congress. Figures like Durbin and Tillis are retiring, while other co-sponsors, like Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) and Rep. Thomas Kean Jr. (R-NJ) lost their seats in the midterms. That said, Congress could be led by two Democrats from a major production hub, New York, if Hakeem Jeffries is elected House speaker and Chuck Schumer is selected as Senate Majority Leader.

articles.content:
Many films about migrants depict their travails. Richly textured and carefully structured, observational doc-fiction “Boys by the River” (“Ragazzi al fiume”), which world premieres in IDFA ’s Envision Competition directed by Switzerland-based Pablo Briones, captures one day spent by three Afghan asylum seekers in Switzerland by a river which one calls “paradise.”

That said, the film also takes in the pressures of their currents lives and in interview voiceover, a sense of their tragic and even dramatic pasts. That is done, however, with a later discretion and sense of intimacy than found in many documentaries. In a larger picture, “Boys by the River” captures one way so many international documentaries are going: Melding facets of fiction and documentary observation to forge themes and emotions.

“Boys by the River” transpires over one hot Summer’s day near the Federal Asylum Centre in Balerna/Novazzano, the southernmost part of Ticino and Switzerland.

Ahmad visits Farhad in his flat, telling him Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Migration has decreed that, given Afghanistan is considered safe enough for return, under certain circumstances young male Afghans could be deported back there from mid-April 2026. Ahmad is highly concerned, Farhad more nonplussed.

The two friends walk through an industrial state and then a long pedestrian tunnel to emerge in fields and then stunning Alpine forest, with cliffs, streams, a river and a mesmeric waterfall. Joined by a third young Afghan, Hameed, they spend the whole day there, swimming, dozing, meeting a couple and their children, talking in desultory fashion. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Most of “Boys by the River” is exactly that: Ahmad, Farhad and Hameed lazing, having fun at a extraordinary forest river.As they do, however, an fragmentary voiceover hears them talking about the horrors of their past.

At one moment, Hameed, now caught sleeping in the sun, describes how he and some other 500 refugees, as they attempt to cross the border from Iran to Turkey, were shot at by the Turkish place who used real bullets.

To bring larger sense and sentiment to the film, Briones captures images with a larger resonance, such as Ahmad and Farhad walk through the dark tunnel, the green forest ahead of them, which becomes a metaphor for Ahmad’s odyssey from Afghanistan, both geographic and psychological, recalls by a few words from hm on VoiceOver during a getting on for two minutes single shot: “Border, desert,.mountains, forest, police. camps, boat, water, fear , fear of cops, fear of animals, fear of getting lost, fear of dying.”

Produced by two bastions of Swiss film production, Geneva’s Intermezzo Films (“Dreamers,” “Sonita,” “Before Summer Ends”) and Ticino’s “ Cinédokké (“The Chilean,”)

Sonita won the 2015 IDFA Audience Award and Sundance 2016 World Cinema – Documentary Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award. “Before Summer Ends” played Cannes ACID section a year later.

Recent Cinédokké films include Locarno Piazza Grande title "Semret" and Sergio Castro-San Martín’s “The Chilean,” one of the most prominent titles in this year’s Locarno main competition.

Briones fielded questions from Variety as he presented “Boys by the River” at Amsterdam’s IDFA.

“Boys by the River” takes some important directorial decisions such as Ahmad, Farhad and Hameed recalling the horrors of their past in brief conversation or voiceover commentary. Why this structural decision?

I wanted the film to unfold as a day by the river, where we first meet them as young men enjoying that place. But knowing someone also means learning something of what they carry. Some memories were shared at my home, without a camera, once we had built trust. I chose to bring them into the film sparingly, so their past could resonate with the present without defining them through suffering or reproducing the interrogations asylum seekers endure. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Though shot in observational style, the film has multiple poetic details which, for spectators looking for them, could have larger resonance, from a forest robot to a lone apple bobbing down a stream, swept by forces beyond control – rather the state of the Afghan boys. Could you comment?

Observation, for me, happens before filming as much as during it. The poetic elements grow from that attention to reality. One day, while swimming there with my children, an apple floated past us. It immediately found its way into the script. Water flows without borders; the apple makes that movement visible, without locking it into one meaning. The robot belongs to another thread of the boys’ reality: surveillance and control that follow them wherever they go.

Again, in terms of direction, you often shot the Afghan refugees in mid long-shot, against the background of the tunnel or forest, for example. Again, could you comment?

I think we experience life largely through a wide view: we see people within a landscape, notice how they move, then sometimes draw closer. I wanted the film to share that way of looking. The river, the forest and the tunnel inspired me even before I met the boys. Filming them at a distance also gives them space, and allows the moments when we come very close to their faces or skin to become more intimate.

How would you place “Boys by the River” in your career and the kinds of films you are interested in making?

With “Boys by the River,” I could explore my love of fixed frames, carefully composed images, and the passage of time within a scene. I also ventured a little further into fiction, not to simulate reality, but to get closer to it or question it, sometimes even playfully. That space between documentary and fiction is where I want to keep working, though funding categories often try to force us to define and limit a film long before we can make it.

articles.title: George Lucas' Abandoned Star Wars TV Show Was More Important Than You Think, And Could Still Influence the Future
articles.summary: I've always found abandoned Star Wars projects fascinating. There's something a little maddening about knowing Lucasfilm has ideas sitting around that we'll probably never get to see. But Star Wars: Underworld is a particularly interesting case. George Lucas didn't just kick around the idea of a live-action show and move on. He spent years developing […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google I've always found abandoned Star Wars projects fascinating. There's something a little maddening about knowing Lucasfilm has ideas sitting around that we'll probably never get to see. But Star Wars: Underworld is a particularly interesting case. George Lucas didn't just kick around the idea of a live-action show and move on. He spent years developing it with a team of writers, and they came up with an enormous amount of material. We're talking dozens of scripts and stories that were actually being prepared for television. The show never happened, which is a shame. But some of its ideas have already made their way into the franchise in ways fans might not realize.

What's even more interesting is that pieces of this project have already found their way into the Star Wars universe . Fans have spotted connections to some of the franchise's biggest movies and television shows. But there's plenty we still haven't seen. And considering how much Lucas and his collaborators developed before the project disappeared, I wouldn't be surprised if more of those ideas eventually turn up in another galaxy far, far away.

The show was called Star Wars: Underworld , and George Lucas started talking about it publicly back in 2005. He wanted to explore the years between Revenge of the Sith and A New Hope , but he wasn't interested in making another series about Jedi running around with lightsabers. Instead, the focus would be on the people living in the less glamorous parts of the galaxy. Criminals, bounty hunters, gangsters, and corrupt officials would all have their place. Coruscant was going to be a particularly important setting. Lucas even described the project as having a film noir influence. Honestly, that sounds like a terrific change of pace. We've spent so much time following the heroes of Star Wars that seeing how ordinary people survived under the Empire would've been a welcome change. And Lucas had already assembled a serious writing team. Ronald D. Moore worked alongside other writers at Skywalker Ranch, developing somewhere between 40 and 48 scripts according to Moore's recollections. Producer Rick McCallum later discussed more than 60 scripts at various stages of development. That's an awful lot of stories for a show that never made it to television.

Unfortunately, the ambition came with a rather enormous price tag. Lucas wanted the show to look like the movies while producing episodes on a television schedule. McCallum later estimated that individual episodes could have cost around $40 million. That's a lot of money for a television series. The production technology also wasn't where Lucas wanted it to be. He experimented with virtual environments and digital filmmaking techniques that could eventually make the show affordable. But the project never reached production. Unfortunately, Underworld never made it into production. Its enormous budget and technological demands had already created serious obstacles. Even after Disney acquired Lucasfilm in 2012, the project was still being considered, with ABC reportedly exploring the possibility and stories continuing to receive attention in the years that followed. Ultimately, however, the ambitious series never moved forward. Still, the work didn't simply disappear. Lucasfilm had already developed an enormous collection of stories and concepts that could be revisited later.

Here's where things get particularly interesting. Some of the ideas developed for Underworld eventually resurfaced in other Star Wars projects. The proposed series included stories about Han Solo's early adventures, how he met Chewbacca, how he eventually won the Millennium Falcon from Lando Calrissian, and how the Rebellion obtained the Death Star plans. Sound familiar? Those ideas have obvious connections to Solo: A Star Wars Story and Rogue One . The series also explored the criminal organizations operating beneath the Empire's polished public image. The Pyke Syndicate featured in that development work later appeared in Solo and became an important part of The Book of Boba Fett. That doesn't mean the finished movies simply adapted abandoned television scripts. But it does show how Lucasfilm could take ideas developed for one project and find another place for them. There's even a reported two-part story involving Darth Vader putting down an uprising on Coruscant. Another proposed storyline explored Emperor Palpatine's personal life. I can't imagine that would've been a particularly cheerful family drama.

And that's why I think Underworld could still matter to the future of Star Wars . There are entire corners of its development that audiences have never seen. Lucasfilm creative chief Dave Filoni has spoken about how the material remains valuable because it contains ideas created by Lucas himself. The series also helped push the virtual production technology that eventually played a major role in The Mandalorian . That alone makes it an important part of the franchise's history. I wouldn't necessarily expect Disney to revive Underworld as Lucas originally envisioned it. Too much has changed, and some of its ideas have already found homes elsewhere. But there's no reason filmmakers couldn't revisit the unused storylines or develop new projects around the same characters and concepts. We already know that the galaxy has room for stories beyond the Jedi and the Skywalkers. Lucas spent years preparing some of them. It would be a shame if they never got another chance.

articles.title: Jeon Do-yeon on Oscar Contender 'Possible Love,' Korean Cinema's Commercial Pull and Her 'Greater Thirst' for Stories
articles.summary: Korean actors are far better known around the world today than when Jeon Do-yeon won best actress at Cannes for Lee Chang-dong's "Secret Sunshine" in 2007, becoming the first Korean actress to do so. She has asked herself what that should change about the work she picks, and her answer is to stay on the […]
articles.content:
Korean actors are far better known around the world today than when Jeon Do-yeon won best actress at Cannes for Lee Chang-dong's "Secret Sunshine" in 2007, becoming the first Korean actress to do so. She has asked herself what that should change about the work she picks, and her answer is to stay on the path she has always been on.

" Possible Love ," also from Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong, is a Venice competition title that also screened at the Busan and Toronto. It is South Korea's submission for the Oscars' international feature category. Jeon plays Mi-ok, a mask-factory worker whose husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), has been laid off. Produced by Pinehouse Film, Anonymous Content, Nowfilm and Netflix , the film opened in theaters Oct. 23 and has been streaming on the platform since Nov. 6. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories As CMA Awards Prepare 60th Annual Telecast, Retiring CEO Sarah Trahern Prepares for Her Exit, and Looks Back on Decades of Prime-Time Highlights Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Reunite at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game Against Jets

Jeon says the projects she is drawn to are "a little bit different from what is globally loved and known these days, so to speak." She asked herself whether she could say yes immediately to projects with wider global appeal, and concluded "I wouldn't say yes to that." "I think I'm probably going to continue to go down the path that I have always been going down, and go in my own direction," she says.

Her frustration sits closer to home. She says she doesn't know about the American market, but within Korea "the focus is not so much about the story or the project itself, but a lot of it is focused on commercial appeal." In her view, "there is less time being spent on really struggling with what the story holds, what the character is all about," and she says she feels sorry to see that happen. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

She is not hunting for a particular role, Jeon says, but "I do feel that I have a greater thirst for the stories themselves." "'Possible Love' is so significant for me at this juncture in my career, and also something that I'm just so grateful to be a part of," she says.

She found her way into Mi-ok through shared worry. "I thought that the anxiety she harbors in her heart was something that I could relate to, because I also have that as well," Jeon says. Mi-ok, she says, "has a ticking time bomb in her heart, almost, because she's always anxious about when Ho-seok is going to explode," and she and Mi-ok share "a sense of wanting life to be uneventful."

Her read on Mi-ok's pull toward Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), the wealthy husband of a documentary filmmaker, changed once cameras rolled. On the page, Jeon says, it looked like desire for a man she saw as "someone like Steve Jobs who could probably solve all of your problems." In performance, "I came to think that it's more about curiosity," she says, "curiosity about a life that's different."

Mi-ok's resilience felt familiar too. Someone once told Jeon that, in the face of hardship, she is not the type to lie down and cry. Mi-ok, she says, is "the type of person who will get up and try her best not to let go of hope."

Working with Lee again was easier than the first time. On "Secret Sunshine," Jeon says, "the relationship or the mood on set, it was very intense," and "I was so filled with self-doubt that it made communication between the director and myself very difficult." Going in this time, she says, she was "a little bit anxious about how it was going to be, but to my pleasant surprise, I felt so comfortable and so much at ease when I stepped onto the set."

Lee, she adds, "was more prepared for working with me," and the overall mood "was a lot more relaxed than before."

Jeon says she is considering a film for her next project, "but nothing has been decided yet." She says she looks forward to telling greater stories and finding those works.

articles.title: ‘Steps’ Review: Brightly Colored, Harmless Reimagining of ‘Cinderella’ Packs Funny Lines but Little That's Unique
articles.summary: As revisionist narratives that seek to rehabilitate a villain’s reputation, “Shrek” and “Wicked” have set the standard for what this type of alternative fairytale can look like, whether comic or dramatic. The new Netflix animated feature “Steps” follows in the footsteps of those more accomplished predecessors, showing that Cinderella’s stepsisters may have been more nuanced […]
articles.content:
As revisionist narratives that seek to rehabilitate a villain’s reputation, “Shrek” and “Wicked” have set the standard for what this type of alternative fairytale can look like, whether comic or dramatic. The new Netflix animated feature “ Steps ” follows in the footsteps of those more accomplished predecessors, showing that Cinderella ’s stepsisters may have been more nuanced characters than just evildoers standing in the way of a pristine princess. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Taylor Swift Ties Grammy Record for Consecutive Album of the Year Nominations Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate

Veteran animator John Ripa (a co-director on the Oscar-nominated “Raya and the Last Dragon”) joins creative forces with first-time feature director Alyce Tzue for a reimagining of the timeless yarn that introduces new lore — the harmless results are consistently funny, but convoluted and emotionally shorthanded. Here, the spotlight is not on Cinderella ( Amanda Seyfried ) herself, but rather her stepsibling Lilith ( Ali Wong ), an angsty goth-girl type with a Hot Topic look.

Lilith and her younger sister Margot ( Stephanie Hsu ) arrived at the kingdom of Alouette a decade earlier when their mother, a traveling seamstress, fell for Cinderella’s father. A schism in their relationship with their new stepsister formed early — following an incident where Cinderella, afraid of being ostracized, didn’t stand up for Lilith and Margot. Now, as a teen, Lilith loathes Cinderella’s picture-perfect personality. Through a series of magic-driven ordeals, “Steps” sees them trying to mend their bond.

That Lilith and Margot are the only Asian girls in this white society is never addressed in a significant manner. Indeed, a musical number, which gives Seyfried a new chance to sing, implies people in town don’t like Lilith and Margot only because they assume the girls bully Cinderella. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Since Cinderella and Lilith aren't portrayed as mutual antagonists, but instead as misunderstood counterparts, the film introduces Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), a self-centered girl envious of anyone who gets more attention than her. And Priscilla has a henchman, Roderick (Peter Dinklage), who is the film’s most memorable side character — his unrequited fatherly adoration for her driving his murderous determination to please her every command.

There’s plenty of invention here, as Cinderella’s entire story as we know it comes to pass before the film's halfway point, leaving extensive room for “Steps” to take the characters into new territory. It certainly does, but with mixed results.

Given that this story hinges on Cinderella and Lilith’s wish for sisterhood, it’s odd that the 10 years between their initial rift and the present are brushed over so quickly, as is the family dynamic that allowed the grudge to persist. Was Lilith encouraged to develop a relationship with her stepsister? Does Cinderella have a good relationship with her stepmother — a character who is virtually absent for most of the film? By the same token, how did Lilith and Margot feel about their stepdad? Early on, a brief scene shows the whole family eating dumplings together, but that’s the extent of the parents’ involvement.

In an overstuffed plot, the time not spent on developing that familial foundation is filled instead with expected appearances by the Fairy Godmother (a wonderful Bette Midler) and the prince (Daniel Radcliffe), but also a romantic interest for Lilith, multiple chases, and eventually even time travel as a solution to the conflict.

With five credited writers, the script for “Steps” feels like a too-many-cooks situation, with emotional cohesion sidestepped for boisterous action. What they do deliver on, however, is humor. Numerous one-liners, often cleverly mocking the tropes of the fairytale, land with the desired irreverence. And that comedy holds together various more disparate elements that ultimately fail to come across as singular.

Though the kingdom is intricately conceived in gorgeous pastel colors, the character design, while not aesthetically unpleasant, can best be described as standard — the way most 3DCG humans look in mainstream animated features. When Margot (a character with little to do) turns into an adorable, pudgy frog, her design — with her hair buns becoming the creature's bugging eyes — provides a rare interesting edge to the film’s mostly generic visual identity. The brightly colored world of “Steps,” as well as its use of pop songs and the contentious banter between Wong and Seyfried, may work well enough to entertain young viewers, but it doesn't make for a classic.

"It's really hard to do AI well, that's why there is so much slop," said Van der Velden. "AI might reduce your budget by 50% but it won't go to 0%. That's why you've not seen a good AI feature yet."

We all recognized the world he was writing in – it was the one we lived in or if […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Stephen King has earned his reputation as a great American author. King was a child of the '50s who came of age in the '60s, so his stories often had that sense of twisted classic Americana. We all recognized the world he was writing in – it was the one we lived in or if we were younger, saw on TV – we knew the people he wrote but then the twist would come, showing the foulness underneath it all. IT is a perfect example of everything King does so well. Derry is both the stereotypical Maine town and Hell on Earth, a place where all the shadows hide infinite darkness, one that reaches out and snares the heart. At the center of it all was Pennywise and 36 years ago, we finally got to see the clown in live-action.

King in the '80s was the definition of prolific , partly because of a certain vice that gave him lots of energy to write. IT was written in the midst of his addictions and it definitely read like it. However, readers loved it and it became one of the horror books of the '80s and '90s (I remember friends reading it all the time), so when it was announced that we would be getting an adaptation, fans were thrilled. IT was one of the scariest movies on network TV – its success led to more of King's work getting adapted on ABC – and it gave a whole generation a fear of clowns, thanks to one stellar performance.

So, I was an '80s kid and a teen in the '90s. Like every kid, I was aware of the things that other kids were scared of, because we all talked about it and messed with each other, and one thing that I encountered only rarely was a fear of clowns. However, and I know this is anecdotal and you don't have to believe me, everyone I knew with a fear of clowns had read IT at some point. Pennywise the Clown was one of the most terrifying creatures in fiction and he definitely had an effect on younger readers.

When it was announced that IT was going to be adapted for network TV, most fans of the book were both happy and a little disappointed. The disappointment came from the fact that the movie was going to have to be a heavily sanitized version of the book, especially since it was airing on the Disney-owned ABC. IT was one of King's more gruesome books and Pennywise's actions in the stories were brutal to the extreme, rendered in all their horrid detail. Fans were sad they weren't going to see all of that onscreen.

However, casting director Reuben Cannon made the best possible choice to play the clown of all our nightmares in Tim Curry. The British actor was well-known and beloved in 1992, the kind of actor that everyone loved in whatever he was in. His turn as the main villain of the flim Legend showed that he could play evil with bone-chilling accuracy, showing his versatility. Curry stepped into the role of Pennywise and just embodied it, as only a great actor can. King may have created the monstrous clown, but it was Curry who figured out what he would be in live-action.

The best actors lose themselves completely in their role, to the extent that you can't recognize them. Tim Curry was a handsome, charming, erudite man and he disappeared completely into Pennywise. He took everything that clowns did to entertain children and twisted it, with Curry finding new ways to show that clowns weren't funny, actually, they were blood-curdling monsters who would tear you limb from limb at any second. That was Tim Curry as Pennywise and it helped make the IT miniseries into much watch TV.

My friends and I all watched it the night each episode released and a funny thing happened at school in the days ahead – a lot of people were talking about how scary clowns were. Suddenly, that phobia that I only rarely encountered became something of a epidemic. It was a turning point in the perception of clowns. The fear of clowns had always been there, but it's one of those phobias that was mocked a lot. Kids like me grew up watching Bozo the Clown on WGN, so for a lot of us, the fear of clowns was weird because we felt there was nothing to be afraid of.

After Tim Curry as Pennywise, all of that changed. Speaking of Bozo, Curry's Pennywise's appearance was based on the famous clown, which is why the role worked so well in frightening viewers. We had grown up with a clown that looked like Pennywise, so to see that twisted into something terrifying was a big change that also tickled a certain part of our brains. I have a feeling that Curry and director Tommy Lee Wallace did this on purpose, taking one of the most well-known children's entertainers of the past and using it as a starting point.

IT was a smashing success, even if the critical reception was mixed. It aired during November sweeps week and it certainly swept. Part One was in 17.5 million homes, and Part Two actually increased viewership by two million. While I can't one hundred percent say it was word of mouth about Curry's performance as Pennywise that got those viewers, I think the proof is in the cultural cachet his interpretation of the character has. He made an entire generation afraid of clowns, to the extent that it's become a much more common phobia.

IT would get a second adaptation in 2017 with Chapter Two hitting in 2019. Bill Skarsgård played Pennywise and he did a great job, with the prequel series IT: Welcome to Derry about to return for a second season. While the movie and series is better than the original miniseries in a lot of ways, there's one thing missing – Tim Curry. For an entire generation of Stephen King fans, Curry's Pennywise is the canon version. As good as Skarsgård's version is – and he's very good – he will never be Curry.

It's honestly hard to describe to you how big IT was. I know you've read the phrase "entire generation" numerous times in your life and it was hyperbole, but in this case, it fits. Curry's Pennywise was so good, so scary, that even in a sanitized version of the tale, he was still bloodcurdling. He made the miniseries legendary, almost singlehandedly making a whole generation afraid of clowns.

What did you think of Curry's performance as Pennywise? Did it play a formative role in making you afraid of clowns? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.title: 5 Video Game Movies That Should Have Started Franchises (I’m Still Upset About #1)
articles.summary: The idea of adapting popular video games into movies has been around almost as long as video games themselves. As soon as well-defined stories were incorporated into the medium of games, there was clear potential for crossover onto the big screen. Those considered the best video game movies are the ones that manage to successfully […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The idea of adapting popular video games into movies has been around almost as long as video games themselves. As soon as well-defined stories were incorporated into the medium of games, there was clear potential for crossover onto the big screen. Those considered the best video game movies are the ones that manage to successfully translate the appeal of the games into a compelling blockbuster, which, naturally, varies in difficulty depending on the source material. All too often, this translation is the biggest stumbling block, and it has led to many video game movies struggling to impress their target audience.

Just as there are many video game movie adaptations that are better than many fans will admit, there are also those whose potential was untapped. In many cases, video game movies laid the foundations for further films in a franchise, but fell short of delivering the success that would warrant a big-budget follow-up. Each of the following video game movies deserved to start a whole movie franchise of adaptations of their source material, but, for one reason or another, these potential franchises simply failed to materialize.

Historically speaking, video game adaptations have often struggled to capture the appeal of their source material. Detective Pikachu , on the other hand, brilliantly demonstrated just how much potential there was in bringing Pokémon to life in live-action. Rather than simply recreating the formula of the games or the animated show, the movie was only loosely based on the game of the same name, instead elaborating on the basic premise of the iconic Pokémon character acting as a detective.

By putting a beloved franchise figure at its core (voiced excellently by Ryan Reynolds, no less), and telling its story against the backdrop of Ryme City, which felt remarkably lived-in, Detective Pikachu laid the foundation for a franchise of Pokémon -adjacent stories that had their own unique style. Despite a handful of minor shortcomings, Detective Pikachu was a brilliant adaptation of the video game source material. A sequel was announced, but years have now passed without any significant updates, leading many to believe it has quietly gotten stuck in development hell. It's a shame, too, because Detective Pikachu had obvious franchise potential.

Of all the notoriously hated movies of the '00s based on video games — and there's actually more than some people would suspect — 2008's Max Payne might just be one of the worst. Taking the groundbreaking and well-loved video game series of the same name and bringing it to life in live-action was a move that fans had spent years clamoring for, but the execution was decidedly underwhelming. Mark Wahlberg's turn as Payne alongside Mila Kunis in a supporting role was not enough to rescue the movie's lackluster script, and Max Payne was, by most standards, a huge waste of potential.

While that disappointment was naturally the reason a franchise never materialized, this was a mistake. Instead, taking the first film's shortcomings and shoring them up by making a superior sequel could have both pleased fans and capitalized on the narrative strength of the source material. It's understandable that no studio wanted to take a risk on a sequel, but with Wahlberg starring, a Max Payne franchise could have become the sort of gritty, action-heavy success that later made John Wick a household name. Instead, the standalone movie is remembered as another failed video game adaptation.

The idea of adapting beloved arcade games into movies might seem strange to many. Classic arcade titles aren't exactly known for their compelling narratives, but there have been a few movies based on these games that have actually been pretty impressive. 2018's Rampage took the most basic ideas from the arcade games and brought them to life as a big-budget action movie. Perhaps the most important addition to this formula, and the catalyst for Rampage 's success, was the casting of Dwayne Johnson as the film's human lead.

Just as the original games were influenced by the monster movies of yesteryear such as King Kong and Godzilla , Rampage managed to recapture that same vibe, just with a little added levity. Giving Dwayne Johnson free rein to deliver bombastic action spectacle has long been a winning idea for Hollywood, and Rampage was no different. The movie had clear potential for growth, as sequels could establish new monsters and give audiences even more large-scale destruction. However, as production on any follow-up has yet to be announced, it seems that Rampage is doomed to become another standalone video game movie that didn't get to live up to its franchise potential.

Assassin's Creed is one of the most prolific video game franchises of the 21st century, and its stories span many historical eras. The idea of putting players into the shoes of assassins fighting an ancient war against Templars across human history proved hugely successful, and seemed to be perfectly primed for a big-screen adaptation. 2016 finally saw the franchise adapted into a Hollywood blockbuster starring Michael Fassbender, but the Assassin's Creed movie managed to alienate much of its existing fanbase and, as a result, struggled to achieve major success.

Despite being packed with Assassin's Creed Easter eggs, the movie opted to focus on an original character rather than those whose stories fans were already invested in. The movie might not have got every aspect of the games right, but the blend of sci-fi, historical action, and impressive visual effects was certainly close to nailing the appeal of the franchise. Sequels could have fine-tuned these ideas to perfection, but instead, the movie's reputation preceded it, ruining its chances to establish the franchise it deserved to start. An Assassin's Creed TV reboot is currently in the works.

As a lifelong fan of the Warcraft franchise, I was personally incredibly excited for a live-action movie set within its world. The 2016 film explored one of the Warcraft franchise's most important stories, which saw humans and orcs first encountering one another, sparking the war that sits at the core of most of its stories. While Warcraft was far from a perfect translation of the games' appeal into live-action, it did a good job of introducing several of the key figures in the franchise's sprawling fantasy narrative, balancing a stacked cast against a story that worked on an individual basis, too.

The odds were stacked against Warcraft from the very beginning, and the huge budget necessary to bring it to life ultimately proved its downfall. Its success simply wasn't enough to warrant exploring the story in further films, and, years later, fans are still waiting for the fantasy movie sequel . Being reasonably well-versed in Warcraft lore, I could list dozens of potentially compelling stories and characters from the franchise that deserve the big-screen treatment, but as Warcraft is remembered as another failed video game movie, the movie franchise it should have started seems doomed never to materialize.

Author and Indian lawmaker Shashi Tharoor is making his debut as a TV host, fronting "Itihasa: Ramayana Beyond Borders With Shashi Tharoor," a four-part Discovery docuseries that follows the ancient Indian epic as it spread to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

The series will premiere Dec. 7 in India on Discovery and Discovery+, with one new episode each week. Each episode centers on one of the story's four principal figures – Rama, Hanuman, Ravana and Sita – and examines how depictions of that character have changed from one culture to the next.

With India as its point of origin, the show visits Cambodia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia to look at the shared history and cultural contact that allowed the epic to settle in each country. It also considers how regional history, religious belief and art gave rise to distinct versions of the tale, which successive generations in different places adopted and reworked.

The show arrives with the "Ramayana" already dominating global cinemas. Nitesh Tiwari's big-screen adaptation "Ramayana: Part 1," starring Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Yash as Ravana and Sai Pallavi as Sita, opened Nov. 5 and grossed $147 million worldwide in its first 11 days.

Sai Abishek, head of factual entertainment, lifestyle and kids for South Asia at Skydance, said the team worked with scholars and practitioners from several countries, who also appear in the series. Abishek said many viewers know the Ramayana through the tradition nearest to them, "but its journey across Asia reveals a much larger cultural inheritance."

articles.title: 36 Years Later, Macaulay Culkin Has The Perfect Home Alone Sequel Pitch & It’s More Likely Than Ever To Get Made
articles.summary: Over three decades after its release, the original Home Alone remains one of the most watched and streamed holiday movies from October through December. It's become a must-watch for the festive season, surviving and thriving not just because it's a great Christmas film to watch with the family, but because it's a great movie to […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Over three decades after its release, the original Home Alone remains one of the most watched and streamed holiday movies from October through December. It's become a must-watch for the festive season, surviving and thriving not just because it's a great Christmas film to watch with the family, but because it's a great movie to watch - period. Macaulay Culkin left the franchise a long time ago, along with taking a step back from Hollywood as he grew older, but if the rumors are to be believed, it might be time for a Culkin comeback that would also kickstart the Home Alone franchise back to the top.

This surprising news comes days after Culkin quietly revived the character for a McDonald's commercial , marking the first time he played Kevin McCallister since 1992's Home Alone 2 . The commercial was to promote a new menu item that comes with some great nostalgic merch, but what was more exciting was watching Culkin step into this classic role through this unexpected way. To many, it felt natural and was the perfect way to officially begin the holiday season of 2026. Those some fans will be excited to find out that more Home Alone could be on the way, and its headline attraction has an entire plot mapped out for the best way to make this dream become a reality.

On a recent episode of The Town podcast , Matt Belloni mentioned he received a tip from someone regarding the former child actor that needed to be discussed in-depth. Culkin was spotted recently on the Disney lot and said "Disney is salivating" over the idea of a Home Alone sequel and "extremely eager to make this happen and is actively courting the actor." Belloni added that they believe Culkin's return to the 90's franchise would be a "major draw" for the box office and is "having his ass kissed like nobody's business" to make it happen, even so far as offering the actor another movie that could be his "passion project" just to get him to sign on for a new Home Alone .

Culkin previously offered his thoughts about what a new entry in the Home Alone franchise would look like during an event last year in California titled "A Nostalgic Night with Macaulay Culkin," also explaining how his concept for how a follow-up could occur decades since he last appeared as the character. "I kind of had this idea," Culkin told the crowd at his event, "I’m either a widower or a divorcee. I’m raising a kid and all that stuff. I’m working really hard, and I’m not really paying enough attention, and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me, and then I get locked out."

"[Kevin’s son] won’t let me in," Culkin continued, "and he’s the one setting traps for me. The house is some sort of metaphor for our relationship. [Kevin has to] get back into [his] son’s heart kind of deal. That's the closest elevator pitch that I have. I’m not completely allergic to it, the right thing." This sounds like a great way to add nostalgia for fans of the original while creating something new for young viewers who have zero connection to Culkin or the John Hughes film.

Most fans have been ecstatic about this possibility, but some feel a tinge of bitterness about it, questioning why it took so long for Culkin to return to the series . The topic isn't something new for the actor, but it's still a mild sore spot for him. “What I wanted is to be with people my own age," Culkin said on a recent interview with Mythical Kitchen. "You have to remember: A lot of the stuff I did when I was a kid … I’m not doing ensembles. It’s me. You’ll watch ‘Home Alone’ and I go, ‘Oh my gosh, I’m in “Cast Away,” except he had a volleyball to talk to."

Due to his sudden surge in popularity, Culkin was also unable to lead a normal life. The problem was that once he became one of the most recognizable faces in the 90's, there was no escaping fame. “I wanted to go out and I wanted to date girls, and I wanted to hang out with people my own age. I wanted to, you know, go to a party,” Culkin explained remorsefully. “I wanted to do those kind of things. I can’t tell you how many bar mitzvahs I missed.”

The actor had to work through many things in order to feel comfortable about being a performer once again, and even more work to return to a character that changed his life for better and worse. As far as we are concerned, this is a case of "better late than never," and Culkin's pitch for the series hits all the right targets for a broad audience. While we won't be getting a holiday gift from Disney this year about the series coming back, fans have plenty of time to stay on the "Nice list" while we hope for the next entry in Home Alone to give us and a new generation of viewers the same holiday treat we enjoyed so many years ago.

What do you think about Macaulay Culkin's idea for a new Home Alone ? Is it time for the series to be revived or should this only be for 90's kids to enjoy? Let us know in the comments.
